turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Thanks for fitting me in. So, I’m a medical services manager—I oversee a few different outpatient clinics, handle the administrative side of things, make sure the providers have what they need. I've been doing it a while, worked my way up after getting my associate's, and I actually really like the fast-paced, putting-out-fires parts of the job. 

But the main reason I finally decided I needed to come in and talk to somebody is that... well, whenever I have to do anything that takes real, heavy, sitting-down brain work, it just feels like I hit a massive brick wall. I mean, things like pulling together the monthly compliance reports, or right now I'm supposed to be planning this big multi-site community health event, which involves coordinating schedules across three different facilities, managing the logistics, figuring out the budget. It's really important stuff. I *know* how much it matters. If those reports aren't in, our funding gets flagged. 

But I sit at my desk, I open the file, and my brain just completely rejects it. I'll find literally anything else to do—I'll go check on the front desk staff, I'll reorganize the supply room, I'll answer emails from three weeks ago that don't even matter anymore. I just keep putting the deep thinking work off and off and off, pushing it to the next day, and then the next day. Even though I know the deadline is looming and my team is counting on me, I just avoid it. It’s like I physically cannot force myself to engage with that kind of heavy mental lifting until it becomes a total crisis, and honestly, the stress of constantly avoiding my most important tasks is just getting completely exhausting.

symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient explicitly describes hitting a wall and avoiding tasks that require 'heavy, sitting-down brain work' such as monthly reports and complex planning, constantly putting them off.

turns.doctor_question: When you're avoiding these important tasks, what's going through your mind? Are you feeling anxious or worried about doing them, or does it feel more like you just can't focus or get started no matter how hard you try?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it’s funny you ask that, because my wife actually asked me something really similar the other day when I was venting to her about this whole community health event thing. And I had to really sit and think about it. Because... well, it’s not really that I’m scared of the work itself, if that makes sense? Like, I don’t sit there trembling or worrying that I’m going to do a bad job or that the budget math is going to be wrong. I know how to do a budget. I’ve been in healthcare administration for years, I know these systems inside and out. 

But it’s more like... it’s like my brain just refuses to shift into gear. I’ll be sitting there at my desk—I even got one of those fancy standing desks a few months ago thinking, hey, maybe if I stand up and keep my blood flowing I’d be more focused, but honestly that didn't change a single thing—and I’ll be staring right at the Excel icon on my desktop. And I tell myself, 'Okay, just open it. Just look at the first tab. Just do five minutes.' But it’s almost like there’s this physical barrier, this invisible wall between me and the work. I just... I can't get the engine to turn over, no matter how hard I push the gas. 

And then, before I even consciously realize I've given up on trying, I'm suddenly out in the hallway checking if the fire extinguishers have their up-to-date inspection tags. Which, yes, is technically part of clinic compliance, but it’s absolutely not what I need to be doing right that second! So, I guess to answer your question... I'm not anxious or worried about the task itself, but I definitely get incredibly stressed out and frustrated with myself *because* I can't seem to just start it. I just sit there bargaining with myself, and no matter how much logic I use about how important the deadline is, my brain just says 'nope' and goes completely offline for that specific project.

symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient describes an intense inability to initiate and engage in mentally demanding tasks, noting their brain 'refuses to shift into gear' and 'says nope'.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing this difficulty with getting started on mentally demanding tasks? And does this happen with other things in your life outside of work, or is it mainly limited to these kinds of heavy analytical projects?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if I really trace it back, I'd say it's been about... almost two years now. One year and 11 months, to be exact. I know that sounds oddly specific, but the timeline is burned into my brain because that's when my friend Mark passed away. He was... well, he was a great guy, but he was also the one who handled a lot of the heavy lifting for this community bowling league we were in, and he also did a ton of the neighborhood outreach stuff that I kind of inherited. 

When he died, it was a huge shock, obviously, just devastating. And then suddenly, on top of grieving, I was the one trying to figure out the league schedules, the dues, the venue contracts, and coordinating all the outreach programs he used to run. I wanted to do a good job to honor him, you know? But that's when I first really noticed this... this total inability to get my brain to engage with the complex stuff. I'd sit down at home with his old binders and the spreadsheets for the league, and it was exactly like what happens at work now. I'd look at the numbers and just... go water the lawn instead. Or clean the garage. 

So it definitely bleeds over into my personal life. It's not just the clinic reports. It’s the league finances, it’s trying to plan out the neighborhood block party budget, it’s even trying to sit down and do my own taxes last year. I ended up filing an extension because I just couldn't force myself to look at the forms, and then I waited until literally the night before the extension deadline to finally do them. My wife was so frustrated with me, and I was frustrated with me! Because, again, I know how to do taxes. But sitting down and doing that deep, focused work... it's like trying to run through waist-deep mud. And it all really seemed to start piling up right after Mark died and I took on all those extra responsibilities. I just haven't been the same since then, and it's honestly been a really tough couple of years trying to juggle it all while feeling like my brain is fighting me every step of the way.

I mean... if I'm being completely honest with myself, and I really have thought about this because, you know, people always assume that when someone close to you passes away you just walk around with this dark cloud over your head forever... but honestly? No. I really don't feel that way. 

When it first happened, sure, absolutely. It was incredibly heavy. I mean, we had this huge memorial service for him over at the community center—the one with the big oak trees out front, you know the one? We actually had to rent extra folding chairs from a party supply place because so many people showed up, which just goes to show you the kind of guy Mark was. And for those first few months, yeah, there was definitely a heaviness. I missed him terribly. 

But now? Being almost two years out? I don't feel sad in the background. I really don't. Like, when I'm at the alley and someone tells a joke, or when I'm at Luigi's with my wife having that veal I mentioned, I'm genuinely just happy in that moment. I'm not secretly crying inside or feeling hollow or anything like that. I'm fully present and enjoying myself. I've made my peace with his passing, I really have. We even named the spring bowling tournament after him—the Mark Peterson Memorial Classic—which was a huge hit last year, we actually raised a lot of money for the youth league, which he would have absolutely loved. 

So the only time I feel anything even remotely close to a "heaviness" is literally just when I'm staring at his old binders, or staring at the clinic compliance reports on my monitor. And that's not sadness about Mark, and it's not some underlying depression. It's just sheer, unadulterated frustration that my brain won't let me do the work. It's annoyance at myself. So, no, there isn't this lingering sadness following me around. I miss the guy, obviously, but my mood is fine. It's just the logistics, the actual sitting down and doing the heavy administrative work he left behind, along with my actual day job, that's what's tripping me up. Not grief. Just... whatever this invisible wall is.

She had to verify that the homework was done and put in the right place, because if she didn't check my backpack every single night, I was absolutely going to forget to hand it in. 

So, yeah, I guess long story short, it definitely didn't start with Mark's passing. It's been this way pretty much my whole life, just this... this constant, exhausting battle to keep my head out of the clouds and my papers in one place, you know? It's just that now, instead of third-grade math worksheets, it's clinic compliance reports, and my mom isn't around to check my briefcase.
